newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraqi Kurds take town from rival group.
newsitem.headline: Iraqi Kurds take town from rival group.

text.p: Kurdish forces broke out of a partial seige and captured a key town from a rival militia in northern Iraq on Friday ahead of U.S. peace talks to end the fighting.
The Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) forced the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) to pull back to a mountain behind the town under a hail of shells and Katyusha rockets, witnesses said.
There appeared to be few casualties despite hours of bombardment. Retreating PUK forces poured machinegun fire toward the KDP from the peak of Heibet Sultan mountain nearby.
Guerrillas cheered and waved yellow KDP flags in the streets of Koy Sanjak to the sound of martial music blaring from the group's radio station.
"We will take (the mountain), stop and evaluate the situation," local KDP commander Arif Tayfur told Reuters.
He said his eventual target was the PUK stronghold of Sulaimaniya, near the Iranian border.
Washington, its northern Iraq policy damaged by the fighting, is trying to bring the warring Kurdish factions to negotiations under U.S. auspices.
The fall of Koy Sanjak broke a partial PUK seige of the city of Arbil, the region's administrative centre that was taken by the KDP with Iraqi government military help in late August.
The status of Arbil, a city of 800,000 people and symbol of Kurdish autonomy hopes, could be key to peace negotiations.
Senior U.S. diplomat Robert Pelletreau is to meet KDP leader Massoud Barzani next week for talks on halting the conflict. The meeting is likely to be in Turkey.
Barzani on Thursday raised the stakes of the peace bid by threatening to call on help from Iraqi President Saddam Hussein against Talabani's men.
"Barzani is shamelessly using the Saddam card to blackmail the Kurdish people and the U.S.," the PUK said in a statement.
The KDP strongman's alliance with Iraqi forces in August prompted U.S. missile attacks on military targets in southern Iraq in reprisal.
Washington on Thursday called on the two warring Kurdish groups to end the conflict.

State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said U.S. officials had made the "clear point...that the KDP and the PUK need to move very quickly toward an immediate ceasefire" in a meeting with a KDP delegation in Washington.
Fighting that erupted between the two groups in August forced the evacuation of U.S. aid, military and intelligence operations and threatened to draw in Iraq and Iran.
The KDP sought U.S. assurances that a ceasefire would hold.
"Our question was what assurances we have that tomorrow we will have a ceasefire and it will not be violated," KDP spokesman Hoshyar Zebari said in Washington.
Washington brokered two meetings in Ireland last year between the Kurdish factions but no solid settlement was reached.

The Kurds broke from Baghdad at the end of the 1991 Gulf War and set up a power-sharing parliament in Arbil which collapsed last year in an outbreak of fighting. The area is essentially off-limits to the Bahgdad government because of a U.S.-led air operation to protect the Kurds in the country's north.
Allegations of Iraqi and Iranian involvement have aggravated the feud this time around. Tehran and Talabani deny KDP charges that Iran is aiding the PUK with men and munitions.
